entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Durand of Huesca (died 1224) was a pivotal figure in the early 13th-century religious landscape of Southern Europe, initially a prominent Waldensian leader from Huesca, Aragon, who dramatically converted to Catholicism in 1207. His significance lies in his subsequent efforts to combat Catharism and Waldensianism through internal Church reform, specifically by founding the 'Poor Catholics'—a unique mendicant order sanctioned by Pope Innocent III, aiming to re-integrate former heretics into the Roman fold. His work represents a direct, albeit ultimately limited, counter-strategy to the burgeoning Albigensian Crusade, attempting persuasion rather than pure coercion.

Before his conversion, Durand was a key intellectual and preacher within the Waldensian movement, known for advocating apostolic poverty and vernacular scripture, appealing to a populace disillusioned with clerical wealth. The turning point came at the Colloquy of Pamiers in 1207, a theological debate orchestrated by Diego de Acebo and Dominic Guzman, where Durand and several associates publicly renounced their Waldensian beliefs and pledged obedience to the Church. Subsequently, with papal approval, he established the Fratres Catholici (Poor Catholics) in 1208, an order designed to live in voluntary poverty and preach against heresy, employing methods similar to those of the Waldensians but under strict Catholic obedience. They received a rule from Innocent III in 1208, emphasizing poverty, preaching, and adherence to orthodox doctrine.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Durand of Huesca's conversion and subsequent founding of the 'Poor Catholics' directly influenced the Catholic Church's strategic shift in combating heresy, laying groundwork for the mendicant movement. His work, though ultimately overshadowed, demonstrated the viability of engaging heretics through evangelism and apostolic poverty, impacting the religious landscape of Southern Europe.
